title: The five strengths of mind training
hookLine: fourth point: a lifetime's practice in five strengths: intention, familiarity, seed, reproach, aspiration
carry: five strengths: aim by morning, dedicate by night

lines: HOW DO YOU KEEP IT UP FOR LIFE?
cards: A toothbrush is a lifetime practice nobody calls spiritual. Twice a day, for decades, mostly without thinking, and it works because it's small and it never stops.
How does anyone keep a deep practice going for a whole life, through jobs and moves and grief and boredom? The honest answer usually isn't a dramatic vow. It's something closer to the toothbrush.
Point four of the seven points of mind training gathers a whole life's practice into a short list a person can actually carry.

teach.h: INTENTION: AIM IT IN THE MORNING.
teach.b: First, intention. The strength of resolve: setting the mind, at the start of the day, the week, the year, on the awakened heart. Something like: today, as far as I can, I won't lose sight of others.
The aim, chosen ahead of time. Second, familiarity: doing it again and again until it's ordinary. The commentaries on mind training say that whatever the mind gets used to becomes easy.

teach.h: FAMILIARITY, AND THE SEED OF GOOD.
teach.b: Third, the seed, sometimes called the white seed: doing good, small and concrete, so the practice has something to grow from. Not big gestures. A kindness, a gift, a held door.

teach.h: REPROACH: A FIRM NO TO ME FIRST.
teach.b: Fourth, reproach. This one can sound harsh. It means turning against self-cherishing whenever it shows up, the me-first reflex from yesterday, and saying to it plainly: you're the troublemaker here.
Not shame aimed at yourself; a firm no aimed at a habit. Fifth, aspiration.

At the end of the day, a wish, often made with a dedication of whatever good was done: that it go toward the welfare of all beings, and that this training continue. So the day has a shape. Intention in the morning.
Familiarity and seed through the day. Reproach when the old reflex flares.
Tibetan tradition also teaches the same five strengths for the time of dying, so the practice a person has lived with is the practice they die with. Five words, held lightly, for a whole life.

how: Practitioners of Tibetan mind training use the five strengths to frame a day: setting an intention in the morning, practicing and doing good through the day, rejecting self-cherishing when it arises, and making an aspiration and dedication at night.

o: five vows a monk takes on entering a monastery
five virtues a teacher needs before leading others
five habits that carry practice through a whole life

games.q: the five strengths: tap the pairs.
p: a wish and dedication at night

s: reproach means being ashamed of yourself
it's a firm no aimed at self-cherishing, the habit, not at the person.
the white seed means big, dramatic acts of goodness
it's doing good, small and concrete, so the practice has something to grow from.
Tibetan tradition teaches the five strengths for the time of dying too
so the practice lived with is the practice died with.

games.q: you want a practice that lasts a whole life, not just a good month. what does point four offer?
o: five small strengths, worked into every day.
games.why: point four gathers a life's practice into five strengths: intention, familiarity, seed, reproach and aspiration.

practice: Look ahead at the rest of today, or tomorrow if it's late, and choose one plain intention, in your own words, about how you'll be with other people. Say it to yourself once, slowly, then again, so it starts to become familiar.
Then let it go, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Five strengths. Point four: intention, familiarity, seed, reproach and aspiration, a whole life's practice in one short list. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan stobs lnga: stobs, strength or power, and lnga, five.

carryVoice: Your line: five strengths: aim by morning, dedicate by night. The fifth one waits for tonight: a wish that the day's good goes toward the welfare of all beings. Go gently.
